title: API Layers, Custom Hooks, and Reliable Data Loading
description: Separate HTTP concerns from UI, encapsulate reusable request state in custom hooks, handle concurrent API calls and failures, and reason about safe retry strategies.
learningOutcomes: Separate network request logic into reusable service functions.
Build a custom Hook that encapsulates data, loading, error, and reload behavior.
Explain why Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level.
Handle multiple requests without making the UI state ambiguous.
Use cancellation and stale-request protection to avoid outdated results overwriting current state.
Choose retry behavior based on the failure and operation rather than retrying every error automatically.

blocks.text: Keep transport concerns out of presentation components

A service module owns the mechanics of talking to an API: the URL, request options, HTTP status check, body parsing, and response shape. A UI component owns how the data is displayed and how the user interacts with it. Separating those jobs gives multiple screens a consistent error policy, makes requests easier to test, and prevents components from repeating low-level fetch logic.

steps.title: Define the expected domain shape
steps.explanation: The Post type documents the fields the application expects to use. This static type does not validate untrusted response JSON at runtime; a schema can be added at that boundary.

steps.title: Make the request function reusable
steps.explanation: The API base URL and fetch behavior live in one service function. The optional AbortSignal lets the caller control cancellation.

steps.title: Turn non-success statuses into a clear error
steps.explanation: Fetch normally fulfills when an HTTP response arrives. Checking response.ok ensures a 404/500 response follows the service's error path.

steps.title: Return parsed data rather than a Response
steps.explanation: The caller receives a Promise for Post[] rather than needing to know how the HTTP body is read. The assertion illustrates compile-time typing, not runtime validation.

blocks.text: Custom Hooks reuse stateful React logic

A custom Hook is a function whose name begins with use and which may call other Hooks. It can package reusable state and effect logic without forcing the UI to use one shared component. Custom Hooks do not automatically share one state instance: each component calling the Hook gets its own Hook state unless that logic connects to shared Context or an external store. Hooks must be called at the top level, not conditionally or inside loops.

steps.title: Model the request outcome explicitly
steps.explanation: The discriminated union separates loading, success-with-data, and failure. It prevents the component from treating data and error as unrelated booleans that can contradict each other.

steps.title: Keep a state transition for reload
steps.explanation: reload increments a key using a functional update. The key is a deliberate trigger for rerunning the effect; it is not the server data itself.

steps.title: Start the request with a cancellation signal
steps.explanation: The effect creates a fresh AbortController and switches the state to loading before starting the service request.

steps.title: Handle success and failure
steps.explanation: Success stores the result. Failure reports an error unless this request was intentionally aborted during cleanup. A larger application may surface a richer error object or classify errors.

steps.title: Cancel outdated work and expose a small API
steps.explanation: Cleanup aborts the request when reloadKey changes or the component unmounts. Consumers get one state object and a reload function instead of low-level transport details.

blocks.text: The Rules of Hooks still apply

items: Call Hooks at the top level of a React function component or custom Hook.
Do not call Hooks inside if branches, loops, event handlers, or ordinary nested functions.
Keep effect dependencies accurate and use cleanup when the external operation has a lifecycle.
Custom Hooks share logic, not automatically one shared state instance across all components.

blocks.text: A dashboard may load several independent resources. Promise.all is useful when the page needs all results before showing its complete state, but it rejects if any input Promise rejects. Promise.allSettled is useful when the page can show partial results and report individual failures. Choose based on the product's requirements rather than selecting one method everywhere.

blocks.caption: Choose all-or-nothing or partial results intentionally

blocks.text: Retries should be deliberate and bounded

Not every failure is temporary. A timeout or transient service-unavailable response may be worth retrying, while a validation error or permission denial usually is not. Retries should be bounded, use delays (often exponential backoff with jitter), respect cancellation, and be limited to operations that are safe to repeat. A client-side retry policy should not create a storm of requests when the service is unhealthy.

blocks.title: Do not retry everything by default
blocks.text: GET requests are usually safe to repeat; repeating a mutation such as a payment or create operation may duplicate effects unless the API provides idempotency guarantees. Define retry rules based on HTTP status, operation semantics, and user impact.

blocks.prompt: What is a key reason to place fetch logic in a service module rather than repeating it in each component?

options.text: It centralizes HTTP behavior and lets multiple components reuse the same contract
options.feedback: A service can consistently handle URLs, options, response parsing, status errors, and cancellation for many consumers.

options.text: It automatically validates all response JSON at runtime
options.feedback: A TypeScript response type or service function does not automatically validate untrusted JSON; runtime checks require explicit validation.

options.text: It prevents React components from rendering twice
options.feedback: Separating API concerns does not change React's rendering rules.

options.text: It makes all requests globally cached and shared
options.feedback: A service function is reusable, but shared caching requires a deliberate cache/store or data-fetching library.

blocks.explanation: Service functions reduce duplication and create a consistent API boundary; caching and runtime validation remain separate design decisions.

blocks.prompt: A custom Hook automatically shares the same state instance among every component that calls it.

options.feedback: Each component calling a custom Hook gets its own Hook state unless the Hook connects to a shared provider or external store.
Custom Hooks reuse logic; shared state requires a shared state owner or store.

blocks.explanation: Custom Hook reuse is not the same as shared-state storage.

blocks.prompt: Which are good decisions for a production data-loading hook? Select all that apply.

options.feedback: An explicit state tells the UI what can be shown and prevents contradictory status combinations.

options.text: Cancel or ignore outdated requests when the owning effect is replaced
options.feedback: Cleanup prevents stale results or unneeded work from affecting the current UI.
Unbounded retry can overload a failing service and retry permanent errors that will never recover.

options.text: Call useState inside an if branch to avoid unnecessary state
options.feedback: Hooks must be called in the same order at the top level of a component or custom Hook.

blocks.explanation: Reliable hooks expose an explicit contract, respect lifecycle cleanup, and use bounded retry rules based on the operation.

blocks.title: Build a small dashboard with multiple API resources
blocks.context: Implement this task in your React project. The lesson editor stores your draft but does not compile TSX.
instructions: Create service functions for posts and users with typed return values and explicit response.ok checks.
Create a custom usePosts Hook that exposes request status and a reload action.
Add cancellation or stale-request protection for a request that is replaced or unmounted.
Build a dashboard that loads posts and users in parallel.
Choose Promise.all or Promise.allSettled and justify whether the UI requires all results or can show partial data.
Add loading, error, and success UI; add search/filtering over the loaded posts.
Define one bounded retry rule and explain which error types it should or should not retry.
Explain why TypeScript types do not validate remote JSON at runtime.
requirements: HTTP logic is isolated in reusable service functions.
Custom Hook names begin with use and follow Rules of Hooks.
Outdated requests cannot incorrectly overwrite the current visible result.
Multiple resource failure behavior is deliberate and visible.
Retry behavior is bounded and justified by operation semantics.
The UI supports filtering without refetching on every keystroke unless the task specifically calls for server-side search.
hints: Keep URL/HTTP details in service functions and component-level rendering in the UI.
Think about whether posts can be useful when users fail to load before choosing Promise.all or allSettled.
Cancellation protects against outdated work but does not replace server-side timeouts or a defined retry policy.
successCriteria: Service functions return typed data and turn non-success HTTP responses into errors.
The custom Hook handles lifecycle cleanup and exposes a small, clear contract.
The dashboard represents partial or total failures deliberately.
Search/filtering operates on loaded data as designed.
Retries, if implemented, are bounded and explainable.
The learner can distinguish static typing from runtime response validation.

items: Service modules isolate the HTTP contract from presentation components.
Custom Hooks reuse stateful logic but do not automatically share one state instance across component callers.
Expose explicit loading, success, and error states, and cancel outdated work when appropriate.
Choose Promise.all versus Promise.allSettled according to all-or-nothing or partial-result UX.
Retry only appropriate operations with bounded attempts, delay, cancellation, and clear rules.
